newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PEASANTS RE-ELECT PAWLAK FOR PARTY LEADER.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PEASANTS RE-ELECT PAWLAK FOR PARTY LEADER.

text.p: A convention of the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), the junior partner in the ruling left-wing coalition, reelected on Satruday party chief Waldemar Pawlak as its leader for the next four years, PAP news agency said.

The results of the vote, announced in the small hours of the morning, showed 695 delgates supported Pawlak, 402 voted for Agriculture Minister Roman Jagielinski and 120 backed another PSL leader Janusz Piechocinski.
The convention also overwhelmingly re-elected parliamentary speaker Jozef Zych as the chairman of the party's council.

"I know I made mistakes, but I also know that I did not betray Poland or the peasants," the Gazeta Wyborcza daily quoted Pawlak as saying to delegates before the vote. The convention received his speech with a standing ovation.
The main contender to party leadership, the 49-year-old Roman Jagielinski, criticised Pawlak for single-handed decision-making and listening to bad advisers.

"Collectivness is good for drawing up strategies, but their implementation requires individual responsibility," PAP news agency quoted Pawlak as saying after the results of the vote were announced. He said however, he would take into account the criticism and suggestion his opponents.

As the coalition's prime minister until early last year, Pawlak was accused by critics, inside and out of the coalition led by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), of braking market reforms and hampering privatisation.

A 37-year old shrewd backstage politician, Pawlak remains popular among many farmers as the man who led the Peasants to a strong showing in the 1993 elections and whose policies allowed many of the party's members to gain government posts.

Pawlak and his supporters, representing hosts of small, poorer farmers often worried over Poland's future entry into the Europen Union, have attacked sales of state assets and land to foreigners and repeatedly called for protection of domestic farms against international competition.
Poland is expected to start EU entry negotiations in 1998.

Western diplomats have said a victory of Jagielinski, a major landowner with economically more liberal policies, would better serve Poland's drive for European Union entry than the re-election of Pawlak.

The Peasants shared power under the communist system but have shifted to the right and now support many of the Roman Catholic, sometimes economically populist values of the main opposition grouped around the Solidarity trade union.

Public opinion polls have shown for many months that the Peasants, backed by around 15 percent of voters, are likely to hold the balance of power in the next parliament, with the SLD and the opposition both winning between 20 and 30 percent.
Both Pawlak and Jagielinski have said that should the Solidarity-rooted opposition snatch a substantial vote next year they could form a government with it.
